Greek-speaking readers would also have heard the philosophical sense of logos as the reason that orders the world. The Greek term is kept here as a title because 'the Word' is now commonly taken to mean the Bible, which is not what John means."},{"verse":1,"phrase":"the Logos was God","lemma":"θεός","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"the Word was God","note":"In the Greek, 'God' in this clause has no article and stands first as the predicate, so the clause says what the Logos was and does not simply equate him with the one he was 'with'. Some render it 'what God was, the Logos was'. The mainstream view is that the wording ascribes full deity to the Logos while distinguishing him from the Father; the rendering 'a god' is rejected by most grammarians."},{"verse":3,"phrase":"What has come into being","lemma":"","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life","note":"The earliest manuscripts have no punctuation, and these words can either end the previous sentence ('not one thing came into being that has come into being. In him was life') or begin the next, as here. The SBLGNT and most early Christian writers take them with what follows; many English translations take them with what precedes. On the reading adopted, the sense may also be 'What has come into being was life in him.'"},{"verse":5,"phrase":"overcome","lemma":"καταλαμβάνω","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"comprehended (older versions); overcome (most modern versions)","note":"The Greek verb means to seize or take hold of, and so either to overpower or to grasp with the mind. Older translations have 'comprehended'; most modern ones have 'overcome', which suits the image of darkness and light. John may intend both senses."},{"verse":9,"phrase":"was coming into the world","lemma":"ἔρχομαι","kind":"ambiguity","traditional":"which lighteth every man that cometh into the world","note":"'Coming into the world' can describe the light, as here, or 'every person' ('which gives light to every person who comes into the world'). Most modern translations and commentators take it of the light, since John elsewhere speaks of Jesus as coming into the world."},{"verse":14,"phrase":"made his dwelling among us","lemma":"σκηνόω","kind":"background","traditional":"dwelt among us","note":"The Greek verb is related to the word for a tent and for the tabernacle, the tent in which God's presence lived among Israel in the wilderness. The mention of 'glory' that follows strengthens the echo, since God's glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35). Many scholars think the allusion is deliberate."},{"verse":14,"phrase":"the one and only Son","lemma":"μονογενής","kind":"departure","traditional":"the only begotten","note":"The Greek word means the only one of its kind and was regularly used of an only child; 'Son' is supplied here from that sense. The traditional 'only begotten' assumes a link with the verb 'beget', but the second half of the word is related to 'kind'. 'One and only' or 'only' is the mainstream modern rendering, though a minority of scholars have recently defended 'only begotten'."},{"verse":16,"phrase":"grace in place of grace","lemma":"ἀντί","kind":"departure","traditional":"grace upon grace; grace for grace","note":"The Greek preposition normally means 'in place of' or 'in exchange for', and the sense 'upon', as in the familiar 'grace upon grace', is hard to document elsewhere. On the rendering here, one gift of grace succeeds another, which the next verse may explain: the law given through Moses, then grace and truth through Jesus Christ. Many scholars still prefer 'grace upon grace', meaning grace in unbroken supply, and the question remains open."},{"verse":18,"phrase":"The one and only, himself God","lemma":"θεός","kind":"textual","traditional":"the only begotten Son","note":"The earliest manuscripts read 'one and only God'; the majority of later manuscripts read 'the one and only Son'. Most textual critics judge 'God' original as the older and more difficult reading, and the SBLGNT prints it. The rendering here takes 'God' as a second description of the one and only, not as a reference to a second God."},{"verse":19,"phrase":"the Jewish leaders","lemma":"Ἰουδαῖος","kind":"departure","traditional":"the Jews","note":"The Greek is literally 'the Jews', but everyone in this scene, John included, is Jewish; the group that sends priests and Levites from Jerusalem is the authorities there. John's Gospel often uses the word in this narrower way. Scholars are divided over how to translate it: some argue for 'Judeans' throughout, while others object that this removes Jews from the New Testament."},{"verse":20,"phrase":"the Messiah","lemma":"Χριστός","kind":"departure","traditional":"the Christ","note":"Greek christos, 'anointed one', translates the Hebrew title that gives English 'Messiah', the anointed king Israel expected. Where it is a title under discussion, as here, this translation uses 'Messiah'; where it is attached to Jesus's name, as in verse 17, it keeps 'Christ'. Several modern translations make the same division. In verse 41 John himself gives the Semitic form of the title and explains it with the Greek one."},{"verse":21,"phrase":"the Prophet","lemma":"προφήτης","kind":"background","traditional":"that prophet; the Prophet","note":"Two expected figures are in view. Malachi 4:5 promised that Elijah would return before the day of the Lord, and Deuteronomy 18:15–18 promised a prophet like Moses, whom many came to expect as a figure of the last days. John refuses these titles along with that of Messiah."},{"verse":26,"phrase":"in water","lemma":"ἐν","kind":"departure","traditional":"with water","note":"Most translations have 'with water'. The Greek preposition most naturally means 'in', and the verb in ordinary usage meant to dip or immerse, so 'in water' is probably what a Greek reader heard; 'with' is also grammatically possible. The same construction is rendered 'in the Holy Spirit' in verse 33."},{"verse":34,"phrase":"the Chosen One of God","lemma":"ἐκλεκτός","kind":"textual","traditional":"the Son of God","note":"Most manuscripts, including most of the early ones, read 'the Son of God', and most translations follow them. A few early witnesses read 'the Chosen One of God', which the SBLGNT prints on the argument that scribes were more likely to change an unusual title into the familiar one than the reverse. The question remains disputed."},{"verse":39,"phrase":"about the tenth hour","lemma":"ὥρα","kind":"background","traditional":"about the tenth hour","note":"Hours were normally counted from sunrise, so the tenth hour is about four in the afternoon. A minority view holds that John counts from midnight, which would make it ten in the morning."},{"verse":51,"phrase":"going up and coming down on the Son of Man","lemma":"","kind":"background","traditional":"ascending and descending upon the Son of man","note":"The picture comes from Jacob's dream in Genesis 28:12, in which angels go up and down a stairway between earth and heaven; Jesus puts himself in the stairway's place. It follows naturally on verse 47, since Jacob, later renamed Israel, was known for his deceit (Genesis 27:35). 'You' in this sentence is plural: Jesus is now addressing more than Nathanael."}],"candidates":[{"lemma":"μένω","rendering":"remain (of the Spirit); stay (of lodging)","verse":32,"reason":"A key Johannine word (abide/remain/stay/dwell) whose repetition across John and 1 John carries theological weight that varying English obscures."},{"lemma":"μαρτυρέω","rendering":"testify (μαρτυρία: testimony)","verse":7,"reason":"Translators alternate between 'bear witness' and 'testify' for this word group, which is thematic in John, Acts and Revelation."},{"lemma":"ἀμήν","rendering":"Truly","verse":51,"reason":"Jesus's distinctive 'Amen (amen) I say to you' formula recurs across all four Gospels and is rendered variously as 'truly', 'verily', 'amen' or 'I assure you'."},{"lemma":"σάρξ","rendering":"flesh","verse":13,"reason":"Its range (body, humanity, natural descent, and in Paul the sin-prone self) leads translations to vary widely, and readers should be able to trace the word."},{"lemma":"ἐξουσία","rendering":"right","verse":12,"reason":"Rendered 'power', 'authority' or 'right' in different places; a consistent policy by sense is needed across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation."}]}

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the beginning was the Logos, and the Logos was with God, and the Logos was God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was in the beginning with God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All things came into being through him, and apart from him not one thing came into being. What has come into being

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in him was life, and the life was the light of humanity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There came a man sent from God, whose name was John.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came for testimony, to testify about the light, so that all might believe through him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was not the light, but came to testify about the light.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The true light, which gives light to every person, was coming into the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came to what was his own, and his own people did not receive him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But to all who did receive him, he gave the right to become children of God—to those who believe in his name,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who were born not from blood, nor from the will of flesh, nor from the will of a man, but from God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the Logos became flesh and made his dwelling among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (John testifies about him and has cried out, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This was the one of whom I said, ‘The one coming after me has come to rank ahead of me, because he was before me.’”)

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For from his fullness we have all received, grace in place of grace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: No one has ever seen God. The one and only, himself God, who is at the Father’s side—he has made him known.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this is John’s testimony, when the Jewish leaders sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who are you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He declared openly and did not deny it; he declared,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am not the Messiah.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What then? Are you Elijah?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am not.”

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the Prophet?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “No.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who are you? We must give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am a voice of one crying out in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as Isaiah the prophet said.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They questioned him and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Messiah, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John answered them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I baptize in water. Among you stands one whom you do not know,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: the one coming after me; I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: This is the one about whom I said, ‘After me comes a man who has come to rank ahead of me, because he was before me.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I myself did not know him, but I came baptizing in water for this reason: that he might be revealed to Israel.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And John testified,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I have seen the Spirit come down from heaven like a dove and remain on him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: I myself did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me, ‘The one on whom you see the Spirit come down and remain, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And I have seen, and I have testified that this is the Chosen One of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day John was again standing there with two of his disciples,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and looking at Jesus as he walked by, he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, the Lamb of God!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus turned and saw them following, and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What are you looking for?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (which, translated, means Teacher),

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “where are you staying?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come and you will see.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day. It was about the tenth hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, was one of the two who had heard John and followed Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He first found his own brother Simon and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have found the Messiah”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (which is translated Christ).

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You are Simon, son of John. You will be called Cephas”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (which is translated Peter).

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The next day Jesus decided to leave for Galilee. He found Philip and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the town of Andrew and Peter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Philip found Nathanael and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We have found the one Moses wrote about in the law, and the prophets too: Jesus son of Joseph, from Nazareth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nathanael said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Philip said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Come and see.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said about him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Look, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nathanael said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How do you know me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Before Philip called you, while you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nathanael answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you believe because I told you that I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly I tell you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God going up and coming down on the Son of Man.”

notes.note: Greek logos means word, speech, message or reason. Nearly all translations render it 'Word', and most scholars see John's main background in the Hebrew Bible: God creating by speaking in Genesis 1, 'the word of the Lord', and the figure of Wisdom, which 'Word' reflects and 'Logos' does not. Greek-speaking readers would also have heard the philosophical sense of logos as the reason that orders the world. The Greek term is kept here as a title because 'the Word' is now commonly taken to mean the Bible, which is not what John means.

In the Greek, 'God' in this clause has no article and stands first as the predicate, so the clause says what the Logos was and does not simply equate him with the one he was 'with'. Some render it 'what God was, the Logos was'. The mainstream view is that the wording ascribes full deity to the Logos while distinguishing him from the Father; the rendering 'a god' is rejected by most grammarians.

notes.traditional: without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts have no punctuation, and these words can either end the previous sentence ('not one thing came into being that has come into being. In him was life') or begin the next, as here. The SBLGNT and most early Christian writers take them with what follows; many English translations take them with what precedes. On the reading adopted, the sense may also be 'What has come into being was life in him.'

The Greek verb means to seize or take hold of, and so either to overpower or to grasp with the mind. Older translations have 'comprehended'; most modern ones have 'overcome', which suits the image of darkness and light. John may intend both senses.

notes.traditional: which lighteth every man that cometh into the world
notes.note: 'Coming into the world' can describe the light, as here, or 'every person' ('which gives light to every person who comes into the world'). Most modern translations and commentators take it of the light, since John elsewhere speaks of Jesus as coming into the world.

The Greek verb is related to the word for a tent and for the tabernacle, the tent in which God's presence lived among Israel in the wilderness. The mention of 'glory' that follows strengthens the echo, since God's glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35). Many scholars think the allusion is deliberate.

The Greek word means the only one of its kind and was regularly used of an only child; 'Son' is supplied here from that sense. The traditional 'only begotten' assumes a link with the verb 'beget', but the second half of the word is related to 'kind'. 'One and only' or 'only' is the mainstream modern rendering, though a minority of scholars have recently defended 'only begotten'.

notes.traditional: grace upon grace; grace for grace
notes.note: The Greek preposition normally means 'in place of' or 'in exchange for', and the sense 'upon', as in the familiar 'grace upon grace', is hard to document elsewhere. On the rendering here, one gift of grace succeeds another, which the next verse may explain: the law given through Moses, then grace and truth through Jesus Christ. Many scholars still prefer 'grace upon grace', meaning grace in unbroken supply, and the question remains open.

notes.phrase: The one and only, himself God
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts read 'one and only God'; the majority of later manuscripts read 'the one and only Son'. Most textual critics judge 'God' original as the older and more difficult reading, and the SBLGNT prints it. The rendering here takes 'God' as a second description of the one and only, not as a reference to a second God.

The Greek is literally 'the Jews', but everyone in this scene, John included, is Jewish; the group that sends priests and Levites from Jerusalem is the authorities there. John's Gospel often uses the word in this narrower way. Scholars are divided over how to translate it: some argue for 'Judeans' throughout, while others object that this removes Jews from the New Testament.

Greek christos, 'anointed one', translates the Hebrew title that gives English 'Messiah', the anointed king Israel expected. Where it is a title under discussion, as here, this translation uses 'Messiah'; where it is attached to Jesus's name, as in verse 17, it keeps 'Christ'. Several modern translations make the same division. In verse 41 John himself gives the Semitic form of the title and explains it with the Greek one.

Two expected figures are in view. Malachi 4:5 promised that Elijah would return before the day of the Lord, and Deuteronomy 18:15–18 promised a prophet like Moses, whom many came to expect as a figure of the last days. John refuses these titles along with that of Messiah.

Most translations have 'with water'. The Greek preposition most naturally means 'in', and the verb in ordinary usage meant to dip or immerse, so 'in water' is probably what a Greek reader heard; 'with' is also grammatically possible. The same construction is rendered 'in the Holy Spirit' in verse 33.

Most manuscripts, including most of the early ones, read 'the Son of God', and most translations follow them. A few early witnesses read 'the Chosen One of God', which the SBLGNT prints on the argument that scribes were more likely to change an unusual title into the familiar one than the reverse. The question remains disputed.
Hours were normally counted from sunrise, so the tenth hour is about four in the afternoon. A minority view holds that John counts from midnight, which would make it ten in the morning.

notes.phrase: going up and coming down on the Son of Man
notes.traditional: ascending and descending upon the Son of man
notes.note: The picture comes from Jacob's dream in Genesis 28:12, in which angels go up and down a stairway between earth and heaven; Jesus puts himself in the stairway's place. It follows naturally on verse 47, since Jacob, later renamed Israel, was known for his deceit (Genesis 27:35). 'You' in this sentence is plural: Jesus is now addressing more than Nathanael.

candidates.reason: A key Johannine word (abide/remain/stay/dwell) whose repetition across John and 1 John carries theological weight that varying English obscures.
Translators alternate between 'bear witness' and 'testify' for this word group, which is thematic in John, Acts and Revelation.
Jesus's distinctive 'Amen (amen) I say to you' formula recurs across all four Gospels and is rendered variously as 'truly', 'verily', 'amen' or 'I assure you'.
Its range (body, humanity, natural descent, and in Paul the sin-prone self) leads translations to vary widely, and readers should be able to trace the word.
Rendered 'power', 'authority' or 'right' in different places; a consistent policy by sense is needed across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation.
